assumptions: The evaluated offer remains the frozen read-only, human-reviewed exception desk for one or two inverter families; remote control, technician dispatch, and consumer subscriptions are outside the initial model.
The intended payer is an installer or O&M firm that contractually absorbs support, warranty, labour, or unreimbursed travel cost; installers that profit from every field visit are not assumed buyers.

The proposed 1,500-3,000 PLN pilot and subsequent 3-6 PLN per connected site with a 500 PLN monthly minimum are hypotheses, not evidence of willingness to pay, retention, or viable fully loaded margins.
Access to the family company supports observation and a first pilot but is not treated as independent demand, repeatable distribution, or representative operational data.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Obtain at least three paid 90-day pilots from unrelated installers with pre-pilot baselines and auditable results showing net internal support-cost savings above the fee, sub-three-month contribution payback, renewal at the proposed recurring price, retained connected sites, acceptable false-positive and false-negative rates, brand-specific API cost and coverage, and measured cash plus founder-hour CAC from a repeatable acquisition route.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The candidate correctly narrows the opportunity from commodity monitoring to exception triage and evidence assembly for firms that bear post-sale support cost. Regulator-reported problem categories and bundled care services make that workflow plausible, but the packet does not show that reconciling portals, documents, and service history is a frequent or costly bottleneck, or that the proposed evidence pack improves decisions over existing tools.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Prosumer disputes and paid consumer care plans establish real problem types and some spending on service outcomes, not installer demand for standalone triage. The dispute pool is small and self-selected, installer support incidence and cost are unknown, and some installers may prefer billable visits; no unrelated installer has paid or renewed at the proposed price.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: A fixed paid pilot followed by recurring per-site revenue is testable and field work is appropriately excluded from SaaS margin. However, the 3-6 PLN site price, 500 PLN minimum, 60-75% fully loaded gross-margin target, payback, retention, CAC, and churn are all unvalidated; fixed and usage-based OEM API charges can consume small-fleet revenue, and the packet's own illustrative economics require roughly 265,000 paying sites for the founder outcome without an evidenced route to that scale.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Poland's more than 1.6 million prosumer installations create a large underlying asset base, and targeting regional firms with several hundred supported sites is usefully specific. Yet neither the UDT registry nor the fleet count identifies how many firms retain costly support obligations, compatible credentials, and budget, so the economically serviceable beachhead is unquantified and may be much smaller than the headline installed base.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: The narrow evidence-pack workflow may be less directly served than generic monitoring, but SolarEdge already bundles monitoring and alerts, SOLARMAN markets multi-vendor diagnosis and maintenance suggestions, and Otovo bundles remote troubleshooting, warranty handling, and coordination. The family-company pilot gives access, not a privileged market position, and no exclusive channel, contract, or demonstrated workflow superiority supports beachhead domination.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful exception desk could extend across inverter vendors, warranty and DSO workflows, additional installer portfolios, and nearby geographies. Each adjacency also adds vendor-specific integration, consent, data-protection, security, language, and liability burden, while incumbents already cover broad O&M functions; expansion is plausible but not yet made easier by a proven beachhead asset.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: The packet explicitly undermines raw telemetry and generic anomaly detection as moats: legal access rights, commercial APIs, free OEM tools, and an existing multi-vendor platform make them replicable. Exclusive labelled symptom-to-resolution records plus embedded workflow could compound, but no customer has granted reusable exclusive data rights and OEM API deprecation shows that a small entrant remains dependent on upstream vendors.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: A single ranked queue with human-reviewed customer, warranty, or DSO evidence could save staff time and reduce avoidable visits. The candidate provides no measured time saving, resolution improvement, error rate, or cost reduction versus staff using free OEM portals and templates, while SOLARMAN already claims causes and maintenance guidance; a behaviour-changing advantage is therefore only hypothesised.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: The large installed fleet, recurring service issues, demonstrated consumer care offers, and Data Act sharing rights create a reasonable opening for aftermarket support tooling. Timing is mixed because API pricing and migration increase costs, privacy and cybersecurity duties remain, and capable OEM and service incumbents are already active rather than leaving an uncontested window.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The founder has unusually cheap access to one family-company pilot and can test direct outreach to a bounded set of firms. That route is not independent or scalable evidence: the UDT registry identifies certified individuals rather than portfolio-owning buyers, no conversion or CAC is measured, and Otovo's paid portfolio-access deal is direct evidence that aggregated access may be costly.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A manual, read-only pilot for one portfolio fits the founder's data and automation skills, 15-20 weekly hours, and a sub-30,000 PLN validation cap. Production across vendors introduces API maintenance, consent, GDPR, cybersecurity, professional-liability, response-time, and triage-error exposure; the packet estimates 180,000 PLN for the broader build and says national multi-vendor operations exceed the founder's part-time capacity without paid pilots, hiring, or a cofounder.

highest_value_structural_change: Replace the low-ARPU standalone software proposition with a contractually embedded portfolio workflow for independent support-burdened installers or O&M firms: price against verified internal cost saved at a materially sufficient portfolio fee, secure rights to reuse labelled resolution outcomes, and make renewal and portfolio onboarding part of the same agreement. This would align the payer's economics while giving distribution and the proposed data advantage a contractual basis.
main_structural_strength: The founder can run a narrowly scoped, low-capital, instrumented concierge test inside a real renewable-energy service workflow, and the frozen design correctly focuses on resolution evidence rather than duplicating basic telemetry alerts.
primary_score_limiter: There is no evidence that unrelated Polish installers will pay and renew for enough verified net support savings to support the proposed price, margins, CAC, or required site scale, while several incumbent products already cover much of the workflow.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: SolarEdge supplies lifetime-free monitoring and alerts, SOLARMAN already markets multi-vendor AI-assisted O&M and diagnosis, and Otovo sells bundled monitoring and service while using paid portfolio-access transactions; together these facts contradict novelty, free distribution, and easy software-like economics for a standalone triage layer.
